user_input: What immunities and privileges are entitled to a witness before a commission of inquiry?
response: A witness before a commission of inquiry is entitled to the same immunities and privileges as if he were a witness before the High Court (Chapter 23, Article 283, p.183).

A witness before a commission of inquiry is entitled to the same
immunities and privileges as if he were a witness before the High Court.

(1) A commission of inquiry shall have the powers, rights and privileges
of the High Court or a Justice of the High Court at a trial, in respect of -
(a) enforcing the attendance of witnesses and examining them on
oath, affirmation or otherwise;
(b) compelling the production of documents; and
(c) the issue of a commission or request to examine witnesses
abroad.
(2) A sole commissioner or a member of a commission of inquiry shall
not be liable to any action or suit in respect of any matter or thing done
by him in the performance of his function as a commissioner or member.

(1) Any person whose conduct is the subject of inquiry by a commission
of inquiry, or who may, in any way be implicated or concerned in the
matter under inquiry, is entitled to be represented by a lawyer at the
inquiry; and any other person who may consider it desirable that he
should be represented by a lawyer shall be allowed to be so represented.
(2) A person referred to in clause (1) of this article may also be assisted
by such other expert as may be reasonably necessary for the purpose of
protecting his interests at the inquiry.

(1) The powers of the Commission shall be defined by Act of Parliament
and shall include the power
(a) to issue subpoenas requiring the attendance of any person
before the Commission and the production of any document or
record relevant to any investigation by the Commission.
(b) to cause any person contemptuous of any such subpoena to be
prosecuted before a competent Court;
(c) to question any person in respect of any subject matter under
investigation before the Commission;
(d) to require any person to disclose truthfully and frankly any
information within his knowledge relevant to any investigation by
the Commissioner.
(2) The Commissioner shall not investigate-
(a) a matter which is pending before a court or judicial tribunal; or
(b) a matter involving the relations or dealings between the
Government and any other Government or an international
organisation; or
(c) a matter relating to the exercise of the prerogative of mercy.

(1) Except as may be otherwise ordered by the commission in the

(2) Subject to the provisions of this Chapter, the Rules of Court

constitutional instrument, make rules regulating the practice and
procedure of all commissions of inquiry and for appeals from
commissions of inquiry.

user_input: What is the age threshold for defining a child according to Article 28 of the Ghanaian Constitution?
response: According to Article 28, Section (5) of the Ghanaian Constitution, a "child" is defined as a person below the age of eighteen years (Chapter 5, Article 28, p. 47).

assistance and maintenance as is necessary for its development

of the child in accordance with law;
(b) every child, whether or not born in wedlock, shall be entitled

user_input: What are the main sections covered regarding the Superior Courts as outlined in this part of the constitution?
response:
The main sections covered regarding the Superior Courts as outlined in this part of the constitution include:

1. Composition of the Judiciary:
   - The Judiciary consists of Superior Courts of Judicature, which include the Supreme Court, the Court of Appeal, and the High Court along with Regional Tribunals.
   - There are also lower courts or tribunals that Parliament may establish by law (Article 126, p.108).

2. Status and Powers of Superior Courts:
   - The Superior Courts are superior courts of record with powers to commit for contempt and all powers vested in courts of record before the constitution's enforcement.
   - They may issue orders and directions to enforce any judgment, decree, or order within their jurisdiction (Article 126, p.108).

3. Public Proceedings:
   - Court proceedings are generally held in public unless otherwise ordered in the interest of public morality, safety, or order (Article 126, p.108).

4. Continuity of Courts and Pending Proceedings:
   - The Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, and High Court existing before the constitution’s commencement are deemed established under it and perform their specified functions.
   - Pending proceedings in these courts may continue and be completed (Part 3, Section 3, p.198).

5. Use of Seals and Forms:
   - Existing seals of the Superior Courts and prescribed forms continue to be used until new provisions are made (Part 4, Section 16, p.203).

6. Structure and Qualification of the High Court:
   - The High Court consists of the Chief Justice, at least twenty Justices, and other Justices requested by the Chief Justice.
   - It may be constituted in various ways for trials including by single Justice, Justice with jury, with assessors, or three Justices for treason charges.
   - Justices must be persons of high moral character, proven integrity, and have at least ten years' standing as a lawyer (Article 139, p.114).

7. Jurisdiction of the High Court:
   - The High Court has broad jurisdiction in civil, criminal, original, appellate, and other matters.
   - It enforces Fundamental Human Rights and Freedoms.
   - It cannot convict for offences other than treason in treason trials.
   - A Justice may exercise jurisdiction in court or chambers.
   - The High Court holds all powers of the court from which an appeal is brought (Article 140, p.115).

These sections comprehensively outline the structure, powers, and functioning of the Superior Courts under the constitution (Articles 126, 139, 140; Part 3, Section 3; Part 4, Section 16).

response: The voting requirement for matters in Parliament according to the Constitution is that matters shall be determined by the votes of the majority of members present and voting, with at least half of all the members of Parliament present. The State should take the following measures regarding the integration of customary values into national life:

1. Encourage the integration of appropriate customary values through formal and informal education and consciously introduce cultural dimensions to relevant aspects of national planning.
2. Adapt and develop appropriate customary and cultural values as an integral part of societal growth, ensuring that traditional practices injurious to health and well-being are abolished.
3. Foster the development of Ghanaian languages and pride in Ghanaian culture.
4. Endeavour to preserve and protect places of historical interest and artifacts.

These measures are outlined in Chapter 6, Article 39, Page 58.

user_input: What three conditions must be met when discretionary power is vested in any person or authority according to the Constitution?
response:
According to Article 296 in Chapter 26 (p.195) of the Constitution, when discretionary power is vested in any person or authority, the following three conditions must be met:

(a) The discretionary power shall be deemed to imply a duty to be fair and candid.

(b) The exercise of the discretionary power shall not be arbitrary, capricious, or biased either by resentment, prejudice, or personal dislike and shall be in accordance with due process of law.

(c) Where the person or authority is not a judge or other judicial officer, there shall be published by constitutional instrument or statutory instrument, regulations that are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution or other law to govern the exercise of the discretionary power.

Before the State can compulsorily take possession of or acquire any property, the following conditions must be satisfied according to Chapter 5, Article 20 (p.41):

1. The taking of possession or acquisition must be necessary in the interest of:
   - Defence,

   - Public order,
   - Public morality,
   - Public health,
   - Town and country planning, or
   - The development or utilization of property in a manner that promotes the public benefit.

2. The necessity for the acquisition must be clearly stated and must provide reasonable justification for causing any hardship that may result to any person who has an interest in or right over the property.

- The prompt payment of fair and adequate compensation, and
- A right of access to the High Court for any person with an interest or right over the property, whether directly or on appeal, to determine their interest or right and the amount of compensation entitled (Chapter 5, Article 20, p.41).

user_input: What are the main topics covered in Chapter 21 of the constitution?
response:
The main topics covered in Chapter 21 of the constitution include:

1. Public Lands and their Vesting - Article 257 discusses the vesting of all public lands in Ghana in the President on behalf of the people of Ghana, including definitions and exceptions, especially relating to lands in the Northern, Upper East, and Upper West Regions (Article 257, p.167).

2. Stool Lands - Article 267 addresses the vesting of stool lands in the appropriate stool on behalf of its subjects, the establishment of the Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands, regulation and revenue disbursement of stool lands, and dispute resolution regarding land disposition or development (Article 267, p.173).

3. Lands Commission - Article 259 outlines the composition and appointment of the Lands Commission, including representation from various bodies and the appointment of a chairman and executive secretary (Article 259, p.169).

4. Natural Resource Exploitation and Parliamentary Oversight - Article 268 covers the requirement for parliamentary ratification of transactions involving rights or concessions for exploiting minerals, water, or other natural resources, with provisions for possible exemptions by Parliament (Article 268, p.175).

5. Establishment of Commissions for Natural Resource Management - Article 269 mandates the establishment of commissions such as the Minerals Commission, Forestry Commission, and Fisheries Commission for regulating and managing the utilization of natural resources and coordinating related policies (Article 269, p.175).

6. Mineral Ownership - Article 257(6) states that every mineral in its natural state in or on any land, rivers, territorial sea, or continental shelf is the property of the Republic of Ghana and vested in the President on behalf of the people (Article 257, p.167).

These topics focus on land ownership and management, natural resource regulation, and institutional structures for administration and oversight in Ghana (Articles 257, 259, 267, 268, 269).

user_input: What percentage of votes must be cast in favor of an issue in a referendum for it to be determined?
response:
The percentage of votes that must be cast in favor of an issue in a referendum for it to be determined is generally at least eighty percent of the votes cast, provided that at least fifty percent of the persons entitled to vote participate in the referendum (Chapter 2, Article 5, clause 6, p.26).

However, if the referendum involves the merger of two or more regions, the issue shall only be determined if at least sixty percent of persons entitled to vote in each such region vote in favor of the merger, and clause (6) regarding fifty percent turnout and eighty percent favor does not apply in this case (Chapter 2, Article 5, clause 7, p.26).

Additionally, there is a provision stating that an issue shall not be determined unless at least 35% of those entitled to vote participate, and at least 70% of the votes cast are in favor of the issue (Chapter 7, Article 49, clause 4, p.63). 

Finally, for a bill submitted to a referendum in Parliament, at least 40% of persons entitled to vote must vote, and at least 75% of the votes cast must be in favor for it to be approved (Chapter 25, Article 290, clause 4, p.186).

Therefore, the specific required percentage can vary depending on the context of the referendum, but the most stringent and general rule is eighty percent of votes cast in favor with at least fifty percent turnout, except for mergers of regions which require 60% favorable votes from each region (Chapter 2, Article 5, clauses 6 and 7, p.26).

user_input: What happens to properties and assets that were vested in the Government of Ghana before this Constitution came into force?

According to Part 4, Section 32, Page 208, all properties and assets which, immediately before the coming into force of this Constitution, were vested in any authority or person for the purposes of, or in right of, the Government of Ghana or in the Government of Ghana, shall, on the coming into force of this Constitution, without further assurance than this section, vest in the President.

Additionally, any property that was liable to estreat or to be forfeited to the Government of Ghana immediately before the coming into force of this Constitution shall continue to be liable to estreat or to be forfeited to the Government of Ghana under this Constitution.

Also, where any person held property or asset in trust for the President of Ghana under the previous constitution or for the Provisional National Defence Council or the Government of Ghana for governmental purposes, that person shall continue to hold the property or asset subject to Articles 257 and 258 of this Constitution, on the same trust for the Government of Ghana established under this Constitution (Part 4, Section 32, Page 208).

Thus, all such properties and assets now vest in the President and are held in trust for the Government of Ghana under the new constitutional framework.

response:
According to Article 16 of the Ghanaian Constitution, the exceptions to forced labour are as follows:

(a) Any labour required as a result of a sentence or order of a court.
(b) Any labour required of a member of a disciplined force or service as his duties, or in the case of a person with conscientious objections to Armed Forces service, any labour required by law to be performed instead.
(c) Any labour required during a period when Ghana is at war or in an emergency or calamity threatening the community's life and well-being, to the extent that such labour is reasonably justifiable for dealing with the situation.
(d) Any labour reasonably required as part of normal communal or other civic obligations (Chapter 5, Article 16, p.35).

user_input: Under what conditions can the President suspend the Chief Justice according to Article 146?
response:
According to Article 146, the President may suspend the Chief Justice by warrant signed by him, but this action must be taken acting in accordance with the advice of the Council of State (Clause 10(a)).

No specific conditions other than acting on the advice of the Council of State are stated as prerequisite for the suspension itself; however, the overall removal or disciplinary process involves petitions regarding stated misbehaviour, incompetence, or inability to perform office functions arising from infirmity (Clause 1), and a committee inquiry and recommendation process (Clauses 6 and 7). Suspension is thus an interim measure that can be applied during this process (Clause 10(a)).

Therefore, the President can suspend the Chief Justice:
- by warrant signed by him,
- only when acting in accordance with the advice of the Council of State.

This is explicitly stated in Article 146, Clause 10(a) (p.119).

  (d) To prevent the commission of a crime by that person (Chapter 5, Article 13, p.33).

3. The party is required to satisfy other conditions prescribed by an Act of Parliament.

(1) Every person who, on the coming into force of this Constitution, is a
citizen of Ghana by law shall continue to be a citizen of Ghana.
(2) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, a person born in or
outside Ghana after the coming into force of this Constitution, shall
become a citizen of Ghana at the date of his birth if either of his parents
or grandparents is or was a citizen of Ghana.
(3) A child of not more than seven years of age found in Ghana whose
parents are not know shall be presumed to be a citizen of Ghana by birth.
(4) A child of not more than sixteen years of age neither of whose
parents is a citizen of Ghana who is adopted by a citizen of Ghana shall,
be virtue of the adoption, be a citizen of Ghana.

(1) A reference to the Government in an enactment in existence
immediately before the coming into force of this Constitution, where the
reference relates to a legislative function normally performed by
Parliament or a National Assembly shall be construed as a reference to
Parliament.
(2) A reference to the Government in an enactment in existence
immediately before the coming into force of this Constitution, where the
reference relates to an executive function of the Government, shall be
construed as a reference to the President.

(1) Parliamentary may make provision for the acquisition of citizenship
of Ghana by persons who are not eligible to become citizens of Ghana
under the provision of this Constitution.
(2) Except as otherwise provided in article 7 of this Constitution, a
person shall not be registered as a citizen of Ghana unless at the time of
his application for registration he is able to speak and understand an
indigenous language of Ghana.
(3) The High Court may, on an application made for the purpose by the
Attorney-General, deprive a person who is a citizen of Ghana, otherwise
than by birth, of that citizenship on the ground.
(a) that the activities of that person are inimical of the security of
the State or prejudicial to public morality or the public interest; or
(b) that the citizenship was acquired by fraud, misrepresentation
or any other improper or irregular practice.
(4) There shall be published in the Gazette by the appropriate authority
and within three months after the application or the registration, as the
case may be, the name,. particulars and other details of a person who,
under this article applies to be registered as a citizen of Ghana or has
been registered as a citizen of Ghana.
(5) Parliament may make provision for the renunciation by any person of
his citizenship of Ghana.

(1) Parliament shall enact such laws as are necessary to ensure that -
(a) every child has the right to the same measure of special care,
assistance and maintenance as is necessary for its development
from its natural parents, except where those parents have
effectively surrendered their rights and responsibilities in respect
of the child in accordance with law;
(b) every child, whether or not born in wedlock, shall be entitled
to reasonable provision out of the estate of its parents;
(c) parents undertake their natural right and obligation of care,
maintenance and upbringing of their children in co-operation with
such institutions as Parliament may, by law, prescribe in such
manner that in all cases the interest of the children are paramount;
(d) children and young persons receive special protection against
exposure to physical and moral hazards; and
(e) the protection and advancement of the family as the unit of
society are safeguarded in promotion of the interest of children.
(2) Every child has the right to be protected from engaging in work that
constitutes a threat to his health, education or development.
(3) A child shall not be subjected to torture or other cruel, inhuman or
degrading treatment or punishment.
(4) No child shall be deprived by any other person of medical treatment,
education or any other social or economic benefit by reason only of
religious or other beliefs.
(5) For the purposes of this article, "child" means a person below the age
of eighteen years.
